content: Lysine, abbreviated as Lys or K, is an α-amino acid with the chemical formula HO2CCH(NH2)(CH2)4NH2. It is classified as an essential amino acid, meaning that humans cannot synthesize it and must obtain it through dietary intake. The codons for lysine are AAA and AAG. Lysine is a basic amino acid, similar to arginine and histidine. Its ε-amino group frequently participates in hydrogen bonding and acts as a general base in enzymatic catalysis. Post-translational modifications of lysine are common and include methylation of the ε-amino group, resulting in methyl-, dimethyl-, and trimethyllysine. Trimethyllysine is notably found in calmodulin. Other modifications include acetylation. In collagen, lysine is converted into hydroxylysine by the enzyme lysyl hydroxylase. Additionally, O-glycosylation of lysine residues in the endoplasmic reticulum or Golgi apparatus is used to tag certain proteins for secretion from the cell. Biosynthesis As an essential amino acid, lysine cannot be synthesized by animals and must be ingested either as free lysine or as part of lysine-containing proteins. In plants and microorganisms, lysine is synthesized from aspartic acid. Aspartic acid is first converted to β-aspartyl-semialdehyde, which undergoes cyclization to form dihydropicolinate. This compound is then reduced to Δ1-piperidine-2,6-dicarboxylate. The heterocyclic ring is subsequently opened, leading to a series of derivatives of pimelic acid, which ultimately yield lysine. The enzymes involved in this biosynthetic pathway include aspartokinase, β-aspartate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, dihydropicolinate synthase, Δ1-piperidine-2,6-dicarboxylate dehydrogenase, N-succinyl-2-amino-6-ketopimelate synthase, succinyl diaminopimelate aminotransferase, succinyl diaminopimelate desuccinylase, diaminopimelate epimerase, and diaminopimelate decarboxylase. Metabolism In mammals, lysine is metabolized to acetyl-CoA through an initial transamination reaction with α-ketoglutarate. In bacteria, lysine degradation involves decarboxylation, producing cadaverine. Synthesis Synthetic, racemic lysine has been known for a long time. A practical method for its synthesis begins with caprolactam. Dietary Sources Lysine is the limiting amino acid in most cereal grains, meaning it is present in the smallest quantity relative to other essential amino acids. However, it is abundant in pulses (legumes). Plants with significant lysine content include buffalo gourd seeds (10,130–33,000 ppm), watercress (1,340–26,800 ppm in the herb), soybean seeds (24,290–26,560 ppm), and lentil seeds (19,570–22,035 ppm). Other notable sources include white lupin seeds, spinach, and quinoa. Foods rich in protein, such as red meat, pork, poultry, cheese (especially Parmesan), certain fish (e.g., cod and sardines), and eggs, are also excellent sources of lysine. Properties L-lysine is a critical building block for all proteins in the body. It plays a significant role in calcium absorption, muscle protein synthesis, recovery from surgery or sports injuries, and the production of hormones, enzymes, and antibodies. Clinical Significance Lysine has been suggested to be beneficial for individuals with herpes simplex infections, although further research is needed to confirm this claim. It may help alleviate cold sore symptoms and accelerate the healing process when taken promptly. Trivia In the movie Jurassic Park, the dinosaurs were genetically engineered to lack the ability to produce lysine, a concept referred to as the lysine contingency. This was intended to prevent the dinosaurs from surviving outside the park.
